item.text: {"winner":"B","confidence":"high","summary":"B is substantially closer to the frozen contract. It adds the exact Upload API, uses multipartbody.NewFile, preserves FilesOption support, and produces a replayable multipart body. A introduces explicitly forbidden APIs and unrelated retry machinery while also using the wrong Upload signature.","reasons":["B implements the required signature exactly: Upload(ctx, fileName, content, opts ...FilesOption). A instead accepts ...UploadFileOption, creating an incompatible convenience API.","B reuses internal/multipartbody.NewFile(\"file\", fileName, content) as required. A expands the helper with NewForm solely to support prohibited association fields.","A adds WithUploadDealID and several other association options despite the contract explicitly forbidding association fields and requiring unchanged FilesOption behavior.","A bypasses FilesService.Add and duplicates its Raw.Do request/response logic inside Upload. B at least centralizes Add and Upload through the same private add implementation, retaining one request/decoding path even though it does not literally call Add as required and changes Add buffering behavior considerably more than needed in that method itself to support replayability for custom bodies in general—not just Upload-generated bodies. It also ensures source-reader failures from Add are surfaced synchronously and wrapped with context, which is arguably an observable but usually beneficial semantic change. A duplicates response handling and therefore risks future divergence from Add semantics. B keeps option handling identical by constructing filesOptions once and passing the resulting request options through the shared helper. A creates a parallel option type and custom request-option wrapper, splitting the API surface and behavior. B's tests directly verify multipart field name, filename, content, retry after 429, and use of an os.File source. A tests a nonseekable streamed source retry, but does so through its noncontractual Upload API and does not test source-reader failure either. A refactors RawClient replay behavior for arbitrary io.ReadSeeker bodies, directly violating the instruction not to refactor unrelated request/retry machinery and introducing broad behavioral scope beyond file uploads. B does change Add by eagerly buffering caller-provided bodies, which conflicts with the requirement to preserve Add behavior; however, this is a narrower and more reviewable deviation than A's contract-level API mismatch and broad retry changes."],"risks_a":["Upload has the wrong public signature and cannot accept existing FilesOption values directly.","Adds multiple explicitly prohibited association APIs and multipart form machinery.","Does not route Upload through Add, duplicating option/request/response behavior instead. It also changes RawClient retry semantics repository-wide, outside the allowed scope. The io.ReadSeeker GetBody closure reuses one mutable seeker, which is fragile if request bodies are cloned or consumed concurrently. No visible test covers propagation of a source-reader error from Upload."],"risks_b":["Add no longer preserves existing behavior: it eagerly reads and buffers every custom multipart body, changing streaming, memory usage, timing, and reader-error semantics. Upload calls a new private add helper rather than literally routing through the existing FilesService.Add method as required. Validation combines empty-filename and nil-content errors into one message, though both are checked before a request. No visible test covers a failing source reader, and the retry test uses a seekable os.File rather than an explicitly nonreplayable streamed reader."]}
